# 10 Questions Every Small Business Owner Asks About Payroll in India — Answered Simply


October 14, 2026


[Shashank Yadav](https://salarybox.in/blog/author/shashank87cc9f270b/)


[No comments yet](https://salarybox.in/blog/10-questions-every-small-business-owner-asks-about-payroll-in-india-answered-simply/#respond)


Running a small business in India means you wear many hats. You handle sales, manage customers, supervise operations, and somewhere in between, you also have to figure out how to pay your employees correctly every month.


Payroll sounds like it should be simple. Calculate the salary, transfer the money, done. But the moment you start digging into PF contributions, ESI deductions, TDS calculations, and compliance deadlines, it gets overwhelming fast.


If you have ever typed “how does payroll work in India” into Google or asked ChatGPT to explain salary processing, you are not alone. These are the 10 most common[payroll questions](https://salarybox.in/blog/what-is-payroll-management-and-how-does-it-work/) that small business owners across India ask, answered in plain language with real numbers.


## Question 1: What Exactly Is Payroll, and What Does It Include?


Payroll is the complete process of calculating employee compensation and making sure every rupee reaches the right place, whether that is the employee’s bank account, the government’s PF portal, or the income tax department.


It is not just “sending salary.” Here is everything payroll includes:


Payroll Component What It Means


Salary Calculation Computing gross pay, deductions, and net pay for each employee


Attendance Tracking Recording working days, leaves, overtime, and half days


Statutory Deductions Calculating PF, ESI, Professional Tax, and TDS amounts


Employer Contributions Adding employer’s share of PF (13%), ESI (3.25%), and gratuity


Payslip Generation Creating salary slips with earnings and deductions breakdown


Bank Transfer Disbursing net salary to employee bank accounts


Government Filing Depositing PF, ESI, TDS with respective departments


Return Filing Submitting monthly and quarterly compliance returns


Year End Processing Generating Form 16, computing final tax liability


**The simple way to think about it:** Payroll is everything between “this person worked X days this month” and “their correct salary is in their bank account and all government dues are filed.”


For a detailed walkthrough of the entire process, read our[complete guide to payroll processing in India](https://salarybox.in/blog/indian-payroll-system-a-complete-guide-to-payroll-processing/) .


## Question 2: What Is the Difference Between CTC, Gross Salary, and In Hand Salary?


This is probably the single most confusing topic for both employers and employees. When you offer someone a “₹6 lakh package,” they expect ₹50,000 per month in their bank account. But that is not how it works.


Here is the breakdown:


Term What It Means What’s Included


CTC (Cost to Company) Total amount the company spends on an employee per year Everything: salary + employer PF + employer ESI + gratuity + insurance + any other benefits


Gross Salary The salary before any deductions are taken out Basic + HRA + DA + Special Allowance + all other allowances


Net Salary (In Hand) The amount actually credited to the employee’s bank account Gross Salary minus employee PF, ESI, Professional Tax, and TDS


**Real example with numbers:**


Component Monthly Amount (₹)


**CTC** **50,000**


Minus: Employer PF (12% of ₹15,000 basic) 1,800


Minus: Employer ESI (3.25% of gross, if applicable) 0 (not applicable above ₹21,000 gross)


Minus: Gratuity provision (4.81% of basic) 722


**Gross Salary** **47,478**


Minus: Employee PF (12% of ₹15,000 basic) 1,800


Minus: Professional Tax 200


Minus: TDS (estimated) 1,500


**Net Salary (In Hand)** **43,978**


That is a gap of ₹6,022 between what the company pays (₹50,000) and what the employee receives (₹43,978). For a detailed explanation of every component, see our guide on[decoding CTC](https://salarybox.in/blog/decoding-cost-to-company-ctc-understanding-the-true-value-of-your-salary-package/) .


**Why this matters for you as a business owner:** When you are budgeting for a new hire, always think in terms of CTC, not in hand salary. Your actual cost is always 20% to 30% higher than what the employee sees in their bank account.


## Question 3: Do I Have to Deduct PF and ESI? What Are the Rules?


This is where most small business owners get confused. The rules depend on how many employees you have and how much they earn.


**Provident Fund (PF) Rules:**


Rule Detail


Mandatory for Establishments with 20 or more employees


Voluntary for Smaller establishments (can opt in voluntarily)


Employee contribution 12% of basic salary (capped at ₹15,000 basic per month)


Employer contribution 12% of basic salary (3.67% to EPF + 8.33% to EPS, capped)


Maximum monthly deduction ₹1,800 each from employee and employer (on ₹15,000 cap)


Admin charges (employer) 0.50% of basic wages


EDLI charges (employer) 0.50% of basic wages


**ESI (Employee State Insurance) Rules:**


Rule Detail


Mandatory for Establishments with 10 or more employees (some states: 20+)


Applicable to employees earning Gross salary up to ₹21,000 per month


Employee contribution 0.75% of gross salary


Employer contribution 3.25% of gross salary


Total ESI 4% of gross salary


**Quick decision table for small businesses:**


Your Situation PF Required? ESI Required?


5 employees, all earning above ₹21,000 No (below 20 threshold) No (below 10 threshold + salary above limit)


15 employees, some earning below ₹21,000 No (below 20 threshold) Yes (10+ employees, ESI applies to those below ₹21,000)


25 employees Yes (20+ threshold crossed) Yes (10+ threshold crossed, applies to eligible employees)


8 employees, all earning above ₹21,000 No No (even if 10+ in some states, salary exceeds ₹21,000)


Once you cross the threshold, PF registration is mandatory. Not registering can lead to penalties, prosecution, and even arrest warrants. Read more in our detailed guide on[PF and ESI compliance](https://salarybox.in/blog/pf-and-esi-compliance/) .


## Question 4: What Is TDS on Salary and How Do I Calculate It?


TDS (Tax Deducted at Source) is the income tax you deduct from your employee’s salary every month and deposit with the government on their behalf.


**Who needs to deduct TDS:**


Any employer paying salary above the basic exemption limit must deduct TDS. Under the new tax regime (default from AY 2024-25), the exemption limit is ₹4,00,000 per year.


**How TDS on salary works (step by step):**


Step What You Do


1 Estimate the employee’s total annual taxable income


2 Subtract standard deduction (₹75,000 under new regime)


3 Apply the applicable tax slab rates


4 Divide annual tax by 12 to get monthly TDS


5 Deduct this amount from salary every month


6 Deposit TDS with the government by 7th of next month


**New Tax Regime Slabs (AY 2026-27):**


Annual Income Tax Rate


Up to ₹4,00,000 0%


₹4,00,001 to ₹8,00,000 5%


₹8,00,001 to ₹12,00,000 10%


₹12,00,001 to ₹16,00,000 15%


₹16,00,001 to ₹20,00,000 20%


₹20,00,001 to ₹24,00,000 25%


Above ₹24,00,000 30%


**Example:** An employee earning ₹10,00,000 per year under the new regime:


Calculation Step Amount (₹)


Gross salary 10,00,000


Minus: Standard deduction 75,000


Taxable income 9,25,000


Tax on first ₹4,00,000 0


Tax on ₹4,00,001 to ₹8,00,000 (5%) 20,000


Tax on ₹8,00,001 to ₹9,25,000 (10%) 12,500


Total tax 32,500


Plus: 4% cess 1,300


Total annual TDS 33,800


Monthly TDS deduction 2,817


**Important:** Under the new regime, income up to approximately ₹12,75,000 is effectively tax free due to the Section 87A rebate of ₹60,000. Employees earning up to this level will have zero TDS.


For a complete TDS guide, read our article on[TDS on salaries for employers](https://salarybox.in/blog/tds-on-salaries-a-comprehensive-guide-for-employers/) .


## Question 5: When Must I Pay Salaries? Is There a Legal Deadline?


Yes. The Payment of Wages Act, 1936 sets clear deadlines, and missing them can result in penalties.


**Legal salary payment deadlines:**


Company Size Salary Must Be Paid By


Fewer than 1,000 employees 7th of the following month


1,000 or more employees 10th of the following month


**What this means practically:** If your employee worked in September 2026, their September salary must reach their bank account by October 7th (for most small businesses).


**Monthly compliance calendar:**


Date What’s Due


1st to 5th Collect attendance data, process leave, calculate overtime


5th to 6th Run payroll calculations, verify salary figures


7th Deposit TDS for previous month (government deadline)


7th Pay salaries to employees (legal deadline for most SMEs)


15th File PF ECR (Electronic Challan cum Return) and deposit PF


15th Deposit ESI contribution


Varies by state Deposit Professional Tax


End of month Generate payslips and distribute to employees


**Penalties for late salary payment:**


Violation Penalty


First offence (delayed salary) Fine of ₹1,500 to ₹7,500


Repeat offence Fine up to ₹22,500 or imprisonment up to 6 months, or both


Late PF deposit 12% annual interest + damages of 1% per month


Late ESI deposit 12% annual interest on delayed amount


Late TDS deposit Interest at 1.5% per month of delay


**Pro tip:** Set up your payroll process so calculations happen between the 1st and 5th, verification on the 6th, and payments go out on the 7th. This gives you a buffer while staying within the legal deadline. Our[payroll compliance checklist](https://salarybox.in/blog/payroll-compliance-checklist-for-indian-smes-2025-update/) covers every due date.


## Question 6: What Is Professional Tax and Do I Have to Deduct It?


Professional Tax (PT) is a state level tax that employers must deduct from employee salaries and deposit with the state government. Despite the name, it applies to all salaried employees, not just “professionals.”


**Key facts about Professional Tax:**


Detail Information


Maximum amount ₹2,500 per year (constitutional cap under Article 276)


Who pays Both the employer (for registration) and employees (deducted from salary)


Applicability Varies by state. Not all states levy Professional Tax


Payment frequency Monthly (most states) or annual


**States that levy Professional Tax:**


State/UT Monthly PT for Salary Above ₹15,000 Annual Maximum


Maharashtra ₹200 per month (₹300 in February) ₹2,500


Karnataka ₹200 per month ₹2,400


West Bengal ₹200 per month ₹2,400


Andhra Pradesh ₹200 per month ₹2,400


Telangana ₹200 per month ₹2,400


Tamil Nadu ₹208 per month (approx.) ₹2,500


Gujarat ₹200 per month ₹2,400


Madhya Pradesh ₹208 per month (approx.) ₹2,500


Kerala ₹208 per month (approx.) ₹2,500


Bihar ₹208 per month (approx.) ₹2,500


Odisha Abolished from April 2024 ₹0


**States with NO Professional Tax:** Delhi, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan, Punjab, Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh, Jammu & Kashmir, and others.


**What you must do as an employer:**


1. Register for Professional Tax in your state (if applicable)
2. Deduct PT from employee salaries based on the state’s slab rates
3. Deposit PT with the state government by the due date (usually 15th or end of month)
4. File monthly or annual PT returns as required by your state


Learn more about all[statutory compliance obligations](https://salarybox.in/blog/everything-you-need-to-know-about-statutory-compliance-in-india/) .


## Question 7: How Do I Calculate Salary for an Employee Who Joins or Leaves Mid Month?


This is one of the most common practical payroll questions, and getting it wrong leads to employee disputes.


**Two methods for calculating pro rata salary:**


**Method 1: Calendar Day Basis (Most Common)**


Formula: (Monthly Salary ÷ Total Calendar Days in Month) × Days Worked


**Method 2: Fixed 30 Day Basis**


Formula: (Monthly Salary ÷ 30) × Days Worked


**Example:** An employee with ₹30,000 monthly salary joins on September 16th.


Method Calculation Salary Payable (₹)


Calendar Day Basis (₹30,000 ÷ 30 days in September) × 15 days worked ₹15,000


Fixed 30 Day Basis (₹30,000 ÷ 30) × 15 days worked ₹15,000


In this case, both methods give the same result. But look at what happens in February (28 days) for an employee who joins on February 15th:


Method Calculation Salary Payable (₹)


Calendar Day Basis (₹30,000 ÷ 28) × 14 days worked ₹15,000


Fixed 30 Day Basis (₹30,000 ÷ 30) × 14 days worked ₹14,000


The difference is ₹1,000. For a team of 10 employees, these small differences add up. Most companies use the calendar day method because it is more accurate and fairer to employees.


**What about deductions for pro rata months?**


Deduction How to Handle Mid Month Joining/Leaving


PF Calculated on actual basic salary earned (pro rated)


ESI Calculated on actual gross salary earned (pro rated)


Professional Tax Most states: full month PT if employee works even one day


TDS Recalculate annual projection based on actual months remaining


**For employees leaving mid month (last working day):**


Item What to Pay


Pro rata salary Salary for days worked in the final month


Leave encashment Payment for unused earned/privilege leave


Bonus Pro rata bonus if applicable under Payment of Bonus Act


Gratuity If the employee has completed 5+ years of service


Notice period recovery Deduct if the employee has not served full notice


Full and final settlement Complete all payments within 2 working days (under new labour codes)


For a detailed understanding of salary components that go into these calculations, see our guide on[salary structure in India](https://salarybox.in/blog/salary-structure-in-india-components-and-tax-implications/) .


## Question 8: What Records and Documents Must I Maintain for Payroll?


Indian labour laws require employers to maintain specific payroll records. During an inspection by a PF, ESI, or labour department officer, you must produce these documents. Not having them can result in penalties.


**Mandatory payroll records:**


Record What It Contains Retention Period


Muster Roll / Attendance Register Daily attendance of every employee 3 years after last entry


Wage Register Salary details, deductions, net pay for each employee 3 years after last entry


Payslips / Salary Slips Monthly earnings and deductions breakdown 3 years minimum


PF Records ECR filings, contribution details, employee UAN Permanent


ESI Records Contribution challans, IP numbers 5 years


TDS Records Form 16, Form 24Q filings, challan receipts 7 years (per Income Tax Act)


Leave Records Leave applications, approvals, leave balance 3 years


Employment Contracts Appointment letters, salary revision letters Duration of employment + 3 years


Full and Final Settlement Final payment records for exited employees 3 years after exit


Bonus Register Bonus calculation sheets, payment records 3 years


Professional Tax Receipts PT challans, return acknowledgements 5 years


**Documents you must give employees:**


Document When to Provide


Appointment Letter On joining


Salary Slip / Payslip Every month (mandatory)


Form 16 / TDS Certificate By June 15th every year


PF Account Statement On request (or guide employee to check on EPFO portal)


Experience Letter On exit from the company


Full and Final Settlement Statement Within 2 working days of last working day


Relieving Letter On exit from the company


**Pro tip:** Maintaining all these records manually in Excel spreadsheets is technically possible, but it becomes unmanageable beyond 10 employees. Even simple record keeping errors during a PF or ESI inspection can lead to penalties. That is why most businesses switch to[payroll software](https://salarybox.in/blog/top-10-payroll-software-for-small-businesses-in-2025/) once they cross 5 to 10 employees.

## Question 10: What Are the Most Common Payroll Mistakes and How Do I Avoid Them?


After helping thousands of Indian small businesses manage payroll, these are the mistakes we see most often:


**Top 10 payroll mistakes small businesses make:**


# Mistake What Goes Wrong How to Fix It


1 Not registering for PF when you cross 20 employees Penalty up to ₹5,000 per day + prosecution. EPFO officers can issue arrest warrants. Register within 30 days of crossing the threshold


2 Paying salary in cash without records No audit trail. Violates Income Tax Act for amounts above ₹10,000. Always use bank transfers. Maintain wage register.


3 Not deducting TDS from salaries You become liable for the tax amount plus interest (1.5% per month) Deduct TDS every month and deposit by the 7th


4 Using the wrong PF wage base Over deducting or under deducting PF. Employee complaints and PF department notices. PF applies on basic + DA. Use ₹15,000 cap correctly.


5 Missing ESI for eligible employees ESI department penalties, 12% interest on delayed contributions Check gross salary every month. If below ₹21,000, ESI applies.


6 Not issuing payslips Violation of Payment of Wages Act. Employee disputes during exits. Generate and share payslips every month without fail.


7 Wrong leave balance calculations Overpaying or underpaying during leave encashment at exit Track leaves in a system, not on paper or memory


8 Ignoring Professional Tax State government notices and penalties for non compliance Check if your state levies PT. Register and deduct accordingly.


9 Late salary payments Legal penalty of ₹1,500 to ₹7,500 for first offence. Employee morale drops. Process payroll by 5th, pay by 7th every month.


10 Not maintaining records for 3+ years Cannot produce documents during labour inspection. Adverse orders. Keep digital and physical copies. Use cloud based storage.


**The cost of payroll mistakes:**


Mistake Type Potential Financial Impact


Late PF deposit (₹50,000 PF amount, 3 months late) Interest: ₹1,500 + Damages: ₹1,500 = ₹3,000 penalty


Non registration of PF (25 employees, 1 year) Back payment of contributions + interest + prosecution


Late TDS deposit (₹1,00,000 TDS, 2 months late) Interest: ₹3,000 + late filing fee: ₹200/day


Missing one employee’s ESI coverage Back contribution + 12% interest + potential prosecution


No payslips for 12 months Fine during inspection + adverse order

## Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)


**Q1: What is the minimum number of employees to start formal payroll in India?**


There is no minimum number. Even if you have one employee, you must maintain proper salary records, issue payslips, and deduct TDS if their income exceeds the exemption limit. PF becomes mandatory at 20 employees, and ESI at 10 employees (varies by state). But good payroll practices should start from your very first hire.


**Q2: Can I pay my employees in cash?**


The Income Tax Act restricts cash salary payments exceeding ₹10,000 in a single day. Any payment above this limit must be made through banking channels (bank transfer, cheque, or NEFT/RTGS/UPI). Even for amounts below ₹10,000, bank transfers are strongly recommended for maintaining proper audit trails and simplifying compliance.


**Q3: What happens if I deduct PF but do not deposit it with the government?**


This is a criminal offence under Section 405/406 of the Indian Penal Code (criminal breach of trust). The EPFO can initiate prosecution, issue arrest warrants, and impose damages of 1% per month on the delayed amount. Courts have repeatedly treated PF non remittance as a serious crime because the money belongs to the employee.


**Q4: Do I need to generate payslips for all employees?**


Yes. Under the Payment of Wages Act, 1936, every employer must provide a salary slip showing all earnings and deductions. This is not optional. Even for daily wage workers or contract employees, a record of payment must be maintained. Payslips also serve as proof during PF, ESI, or income tax inspections.


**Q5: How do I decide the salary structure (basic, HRA, allowances) for my employees?**


Under the Code on Wages, 2019 (effective from November 2025), basic salary plus dearness allowance must be at least 50% of the total remuneration. Within this rule, most companies set basic at 40% to 50% of CTC, HRA at 40% to 50% of basic, and the rest as[allowances](https://salarybox.in/blog/what-are-allowances-in-salary-types-and-examples/) like special allowance, conveyance, and medical. The structure affects PF contributions,[gratuity](https://salarybox.in/blog/understanding-gratuity-a-powerful-tool-for-motivating-and-engaging-employees/) , and tax calculations.


**Q6: When should I issue Form 16 to my employees?**


Form 16 must be issued by June 15th of the assessment year. For FY 2025-26, the deadline is June 15, 2026. Form 16 is the TDS certificate that employees need to file their income tax returns. You generate it after filing your quarterly TDS returns (Form 24Q) on the TRACES portal. Not issuing Form 16 can attract a penalty of ₹100 per day per employee.


**Q7: My employee’s gross salary crossed ₹21,000 after a raise. Do I stop ESI deductions?**


Yes. ESI applies only to employees whose gross monthly salary is ₹21,000 or below. Once an employee’s gross crosses this threshold (after a salary revision or increment), ESI deductions stop from the next contribution period. However, the employee remains covered for medical benefits until the end of the contribution period in which the salary crossed the limit.


**Q8: Is gratuity applicable for small businesses with fewer than 10 employees?**


The Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 applies to establishments with 10 or more employees. If your business has fewer than 10 employees, you are not legally required to pay gratuity. However, once you cross 10 employees, the Act becomes applicable, and it continues to apply even if your employee count later drops below 10. An employee must complete 5 years of continuous service to become eligible for gratuity.
